$schema: Full character cast for all 6 stories. plain = accessible description. summary = one-line chip text. description = extended narrative for modal. sourceTrail = scholarly provenance.

characters.name: Medb
characters.title: Queen of Connacht
characters.summary: The proud queen whose refusal to be lesser than her husband ignites the war.
characters.plain: Medb (often anglicised Maeve) is the proud, formidable queen who rules Connacht from Cruachan. She insists on being her husband's equal in every possession — and that insistence sets the whole war in motion.
characters.description: Medb rules Connacht in her own right — a queen before she was a wife. Her defining quality is an absolute refusal to accept inferiority. When the pillow-talk contest reveals that Ailill possesses the White-Horned Bull and she does not, she experiences it not as envy but as a breach of equality. The war she launches to acquire the Brown Bull of Cooley is, in her framing, an act of justice. She negotiates, threatens, bribes, and campaigns throughout the Táin with cold strategic intelligence. Scholarly opinion is divided on whether Medb began as a sovereignty goddess — the land personified, whom a king must ritually wed — or was always a fully-realised literary character.

sourceTrail.earliest: Lebor na hUidre (c. 1100 CE) and Book of Leinster (c. 1150 CE)
sourceTrail.notes: Medb may originate as a sovereignty goddess. Her name may mean 'she who intoxicates.' Multiple recensions of the Táin give slightly different portrayals.

characters.name: Ailill
characters.title: King of Connacht
characters.summary: Medb's husband and co-ruler, whose bull tips the balance and starts everything.
characters.plain: Ailill is Medb's husband and co-ruler. Good-humoured but competitive, he is the one who points out that his herd holds a bull Medb cannot match — the spark of the quarrel.
characters.description: Ailill is a more passive force in the Táin than his wife — it is Medb who drives the narrative. But his role is structurally crucial: his possession of the White-Horned Bull, and his pointed observation that this gives him the advantage in their counting contest, is the direct cause of the war. He is not cruel or ambitious; he simply cannot resist noting, from comfortable superiority, that his wife is not quite his equal in one respect. That observation, delivered at the wrong moment to the wrong woman, sets four provinces in motion.

sourceTrail.notes: Ailill's characterisation varies between recensions — sometimes more sympathetic, sometimes more contentious.

characters.name: Finnbhennach
characters.title: The White-Horned Bull
characters.summary: The magnificent bull who refused a woman's ownership and crossed to Ailill's herd.
characters.plain: The White-Horned Bull was born into Medb's herd but, too proud to be owned by a woman, walked over to Ailill's cattle. His defection is exactly what unbalances the royal couple's wealth.
characters.description: Finnbhennach is more than a prize animal — he and Donn Cúailnge are identified in the Táin as reincarnated supernatural beings, rivals through multiple lifetimes who were in turn ravens, water creatures, stags, warriors, ghosts, and finally bulls. The cosmic enmity between them predates the human story entirely. The climax of the Táin is not a battle between armies but a single cataclysmic fight between the two bulls, which ranges across all of Ireland. Finnbhennach loses — but his name survives in the Irish landscape.

sourceTrail.notes: The bulls' backstory as reincarnating supernatural beings is told in the foretale De Chophur in dá Muccida (The Quarrel of the Two Swineherds).

characters.name: Donn Cúailnge
characters.title: The Brown Bull of Cooley
characters.summary: The only bull in Ireland fit to match the white one — and worth a war to possess.
characters.plain: The Brown Bull of Cooley is the only beast in Ireland to equal the White-Horned Bull. He belongs to Ulster, and winning him — by purchase or by force — becomes Medb's single aim.
characters.description: Donn Cúailnge embodies Ulster's wealth and honour. Like Finnbhennach, he is a supernatural being in his final incarnation — once a swineherd's assistant, now a bull of extraordinary intelligence and ferocity. The climax of the Táin is the single cataclysmic fight between the two bulls. Donn Cúailnge wins — but he dies of his wounds, his flesh left in fragments at the places whose names commemorate the battle. The entire war was fought over something neither side would keep.

sourceTrail.notes: The place-names associated with the bulls' final battle form an onomastic trail across Ulster and Leinster.

characters.name: Dáire mac Fiachna
characters.title: Lord of the Brown Bull
characters.summary: The Ulster lord who first agreed to lend the bull — until a drunken boast cost him his honour.
characters.plain: Dáire is the Ulster lord who owns the Brown Bull. He first agrees to lend it to Medb — until a drunken boast from her messengers insults him, and he refuses outright.
characters.description: Dáire mac Fiachna's brief scene contains the Táin's essential irony: the war that devastates two provinces happens because of a piece of drunken bragging. Dáire is initially generous — willing to lend his prize bull for a year in exchange for fair payment. It is only when his hospitality is repaid with an overheard boast that the deal collapses. His injured pride, and his absolute refusal to negotiate after that, is entirely understandable by the story's own social code.

characters.name: Cú Chulainn
characters.title: Champion of Ulster
characters.summary: The boy champion who alone holds the Ulster ford against the armies of four provinces.
characters.plain: Cú Chulainn is the young champion of Ulster — only seventeen, but unmatched in battle. When Medb's army marches, the grown men of Ulster lie helpless under an ancient curse, and the boy alone stands at the border.
characters.description: Cú Chulainn was born Sétanta, son of the god Lugh and the mortal Deichtine. He earned his name by killing the hound of the smith Culann and pledging to serve as guard-dog in its place. He trained under the warrior-woman Scáthach in Scotland. In the Táin, he is seventeen years old, immune to the curse that prostrates Ulster's warriors by virtue of his divine parentage, and must hold the Ulster border alone — fighting single combats at every ford while the province recovers. His most famous single combat is with his foster-brother Ferdia, three days of battle that he wins, and which breaks him.

sourceTrail.primary: Táin Bó Cúailnge; also Aided Con Culainn (Death of Cú Chulainn)
sourceTrail.notes: One of the best-documented figures in early Irish literature, appearing in dozens of tales.

characters.name: Ferdia
characters.title: Champion of Connacht
characters.summary: Cú Chulainn's foster-brother, pressed by Medb to fight the one man he cannot kill.
characters.plain: Ferdia was trained alongside Cú Chulainn under the warrior-woman Scáthach, and the two were foster-brothers in arms. Medb pressures him — with gifts, promises, and finally threats to his honour — into fighting his dearest companion at the ford. Their combat lasts three days.
characters.description: Ferdia's episode is the emotional and moral climax of the Táin — more devastating than any battle. He and Cú Chulainn trained together, fought side by side, and loved each other as brothers. When Medb exhausts her ability to bribe him, she threatens his honour and reputation. Each evening of the three-day combat, the two men dress each other's wounds, share food and medicine, and sleep beside the same fire. On the fourth morning Cú Chulainn uses the gáe bolga — a terrible weapon Scáthach had taught only him — and Ferdia dies. Cú Chulainn's lament over his body is one of the finest passages in the Táin.

sourceTrail.primary: Táin Bó Cúailnge — 'The Combat at the Ford'
sourceTrail.notes: The combat at the ford is one of the oldest and most consistently preserved episodes in the Táin tradition.

characters.name: Conchobar mac Nessa
characters.title: High King of Ulster
characters.summary: Ulster's king — the man whose obsession with Deirdre destroys more than it gains.
characters.plain: Conchobar mac Nessa is the High King of Ulster, lord of the Red Branch warriors, and the man who imprisons Deirdre from childhood. His role in the Táin is largely that of the sovereign who cannot act — the curse of Macha keeps him prostrate when he is needed most.
characters.description: Conchobar appears in both the Táin and Deirdre's story, and the two portrayals are hard to reconcile. In the Táin he is a legitimate and respected king whose warriors cannot act — the tragedy is structural, not personal. In Deirdre he is something darker: a king who imprisons a child on a prophecy's authority, keeps her isolated until he can make her his wife, and when she defies him, engineers the killing of the man she loves rather than accept failure. His deliberate betrayal of Fergus's guarantee of safe passage sends the Ulster cycle into long decline.

sourceTrail.primary: Táin Bó Cúailnge; Longes mac nUislenn
sourceTrail.oral: Ulster Cycle oral tradition, Iron Age
sourceTrail.notes: Conchobar's characterisation is notably inconsistent across different Ulster Cycle texts — hero in some, villain in others.

characters.name: Fergus mac Róich
characters.title: Exiled Champion of Ulster
characters.summary: The great Ulster champion who fights for Connacht, honour-bound by Conchobar's treachery.
characters.plain: Fergus mac Róich is the greatest of the old Ulster champions, now exiled in Connacht after Conchobar's betrayal of his pledge. He fights for Medb in the Táin, but holds back from facing Cú Chulainn — they have their own oath between them.
characters.description: Fergus mac Róich was once king of Ulster before Conchobar. He relinquished his throne and later went into exile after Conchobar used him as an instrument of betrayal in the Deirdre story — Fergus gave his personal guarantee of safe passage to Naoise, and Conchobar dishonoured it. His honour broken, Fergus joined Medb's court. In the Táin he fights for Connacht against his own people — but holds back when the moment comes to face Cú Chulainn, with whom he has a compact of friendship, and deliberately misses Ulster's forces with his sword-strokes. He is a figure defined by competing loyalties he cannot resolve.

sourceTrail.primary: Táin Bó Cúailnge; Longes mac nUislenn
sourceTrail.notes: Fergus's sword Caladbolg ('hard lightning') is widely considered cognate with Excalibur.

characters.name: The Morrígan
characters.title: Goddess of War and Fate
characters.summary: The shapeshifting goddess of fate and war who tests Cú Chulainn and prophesies his death.
characters.plain: The Morrígan is a goddess of war, fate, and sovereignty. In the Táin she approaches Cú Chulainn in several guises — as a young woman, as a crow, as an eel. She offers him her love; he refuses; she attacks him during his combats at the ford.
characters.description: The Morrígan (often translated as 'Phantom Queen') is one of the most powerful figures in the Irish supernatural tradition. She is simultaneously goddess of battle, shapeshifter, prophet, and sovereignty figure. In the Táin she forms one of the story's most ambiguous sub-plots: she approaches Cú Chulainn and declares her love; he dismisses her; she transforms her rejection into a series of attacks during his ford combats — an eel, a grey wolf, a hornless heifer. Each time he wounds her in return. Later, when she disguises herself as an old woman milking a cow and he unwittingly heals her three injuries by accepting three drinks of milk, their relationship concludes in a truce. She is also sometimes a tripartite goddess — Badb, Macha, and Nemain are presented as her three aspects.

sourceTrail.primary: Táin Bó Cúailnge; also Cath Maige Tuired
sourceTrail.notes: Her exact nature is contested in scholarship. She may be a single goddess, a triple goddess, or a category of supernatural women.

characters.name: Mac Roth
characters.title: Medb's Herald and Scout
characters.summary: Medb's chief messenger — the man who names the only bull in Ireland to equal the white one.
characters.plain: Mac Roth is Medb's chief herald and scout. He tells her about Donn Cúailnge and leads the embassy that attempts to borrow the bull. When his men's drunken boasting ruins the negotiation, the war becomes inevitable.
characters.description: Mac Roth occupies a pivotal structural position in the Táin — as the herald, he is the bearer of information that turns a domestic argument into an international crisis. He identifies Donn Cúailnge; leads the embassy that nearly succeeds; and his men, drunk on Dáire's hospitality, boast that Connacht would have taken the bull by force anyway. That boast ends the possibility of a peaceful resolution. Mac Roth also appears elsewhere in the Táin as a scout of almost supernatural ability, able to watch entire armies from a hilltop and describe each warrior's identity from their bearing and equipment.

characters.name: Lir
characters.title: King of Sídhe Fionnachaidh
characters.summary: The Tuatha Dé king whose children are cursed to live as swans for nine hundred years.
characters.plain: Lir is a lord of the Tuatha Dé Danann who lives at Sídhe Fionnachaidh after the gods retreated to the fairy mounds. His four children are the centre of his world. When his first wife dies and he remarries, the jealousy of his new wife Aoife destroys everything he loves.
characters.description: Lir is the passive, devastated centre of the Children of Lir story. He loves his children absolutely, and that love is the reason Aoife transforms them — it is more than she can bear to witness. After the transformation Lir is grief-stricken. Bodb Dearg punishes Aoife, but no power can undo the curse. Lir ages and dies while his children continue their exile. The story is partly about the helplessness of love against supernatural forces, and partly about the long patience required of those who have no choice but to wait.

sourceTrail.primary: Oidheadh Chlainne Lir (Fate of the Children of Lir)
sourceTrail.earliest: Preserved in 15th–17th century manuscripts; oral tradition significantly older
sourceTrail.notes: One of the Trí Truaighe na Scéalaíochta — Three Sorrows of Storytelling.

characters.name: Fionnuala
characters.title: Eldest of the Swan Children
characters.summary: The eldest swan child who shelters her brothers under her wings through centuries of exile.
characters.plain: Fionnuala is the eldest of Lir's four children transformed into swans by their jealous stepmother. Through nine hundred years of exile she is her brothers' protector — gathering them under her wings in the storms of the Sea of Moyle.
characters.description: Fionnuala is the story's true protagonist. Her function across nine hundred years is to hold her family together when every force attempts separation. In the cold of the Sea of Moyle, storms tear the siblings apart; each time the seas calm, she swims until she finds all three brothers and draws them back under her feathers. She takes Conn under her right wing, Fiachra under her left, and Aodh under her breast-feathers. This image — the eldest sister sheltering her siblings in the dark — is the emotional core of the story. When the curse ends and they die as ancient humans, they are buried together with Fionnuala's arms still around her brothers.

sourceTrail.notes: Fionnuala's protective role and the specific detail of sheltering brothers under each wing is one of the most consistent details across retellings.

characters.name: Aodh
characters.title: Son of Lir
characters.summary: The second of Lir's children, sheltered under Fionnuala's breast-feathers through nine centuries.
characters.plain: Aodh is one of Lir's four children cursed into swan form. He is sheltered under Fionnuala's breast-feathers — closest to her heart — in the worst storms of the Sea of Moyle. He and his siblings endure nine hundred years of exile.
characters.description: Aodh is given the most intimate position in Fionnuala's sheltering embrace — tucked against her breast-feathers, closest to her heart. In this detail the story encodes the special relationship of the eldest sister and her nearest younger brother. The power of the four children as a group is their song — so beautiful that no one who hears it can feel grief.

characters.name: Fiachra
characters.title: Son of Lir
characters.summary: One of the four swan children, sheltered under Fionnuala's left wing through nine hundred years.
characters.plain: Fiachra is one of Lir's four children. In the storms of the Sea of Moyle, Fionnuala shelters him under her left wing. He endures nine centuries of exile alongside his sister and brothers.
characters.description: Fiachra and Conn are sheltered under Fionnuala's wings — left and right — while Aodh takes the position closest to her heart. The geometric precision of this arrangement, preserved across centuries of oral retelling, suggests it carried symbolic weight. The four children's collective endurance is what makes them sympathetic figures rather than simply victims.

characters.name: Conn
characters.title: Youngest Son of Lir
characters.summary: The youngest of the four swan children, sheltered under Fionnuala's right wing.
characters.plain: Conn is the youngest of Lir's four children. In the storms of the Sea of Moyle, Fionnuala draws him under her right wing to keep him safe. He and his siblings live nine hundred years as swans before returning briefly to human form at the last.
characters.description: Conn — the youngest — occupies the most protected position under Fionnuala's right wing. His youth at the time of the transformation makes his nine-hundred-year exile especially poignant: he never had a full human childhood. The four children's relationship with each other is the moral centre of the story.

sourceTrail.notes: Not to be confused with Conn of the Hundred Battles, the legendary High King.

characters.name: Aoife
characters.title: Second Wife of Lir
characters.summary: The jealous stepmother whose druid's wand transforms four children into swans for nine centuries.
characters.plain: Aoife is Lir's second wife, daughter of Bodb Dearg. Her growing jealousy of the four children leads her to strike them with her druid's wand at the edge of Lough Derravaragh. She curses them to nine hundred years in swan form. She cannot undo what she has done.
characters.description: Aoife is one of Irish mythology's most complex antagonists. She is not straightforwardly evil — she is a woman consumed by a jealousy she recognises as destructive even as it overwhelms her. The text records that she wept as she drove the children to the lake, and that she hesitated before speaking the curse. When she attempts to kill them outright, her hand fails her. Her punishment, decreed by her father Bodb Dearg, is to spend eternity as a demon of the air. The story gives her no redemption, but it does not deny her the complexity of someone who chose something terrible and knew it was terrible at the moment of choosing.

sourceTrail.notes: Aoife (daughter of Bodb Dearg) is an entirely different character from Aoife the warrior-woman in Cú Chulainn's training narratives.

characters.name: Bodb Dearg
characters.title: High King of the Tuatha Dé Danann
characters.summary: High king of the old gods, Aoife's father — he can deliver justice but not undo the curse.
characters.plain: Bodb Dearg is the high king of the Tuatha Dé Danann after their defeat and retreat underground. He is Aoife's father. When he discovers what she has done to the children, he punishes her — but cannot undo her curse.
characters.description: Bodb Dearg represents the last authority of the old gods in their diminished state. He rules the Tuatha Dé in their invisible world beneath the hills of Ireland — a king of what has already been lost. When Lir's children are transformed, Bodb Dearg exercises the only power he has left: justice. He condemns Aoife to her own supernatural exile. But even the high king of the old gods cannot reverse a druidic transformation. His presence underlines the story's central theme: that some things cannot be undone, only endured.

sourceTrail.notes: Bodb Dearg also appears prominently in Cath Maige Tuired.

characters.name: Mochaomhóg
characters.title: Christian Monk of Inishglora
characters.summary: The monk whose bell across the water draws the swans in from nine hundred years of exile.
characters.plain: Mochaomhóg is a Christian monk who settles on the tiny island of Inishglora off the Mayo coast. His bell is the first thing the swan children hear that gives them peace. He becomes their protector and baptises them as they die at the end of the curse.
characters.description: Mochaomhóg's function is to represent the new world that has arisen while the children were exiled — the world of Christianity that has replaced the old gods' Ireland. His bell across the water draws the swans not because it is beautiful but because it speaks to something they cannot name. He recognises them as the children of Lir and cares for them as parishioners, fashioning silver chains to keep them together. When a Connacht king tries to take the swans as a gift for his queen, Mochaomhóg refuses — triggering the end of the curse. He baptises the four as they die, ancient and barely alive. His final act is to bury them standing, with Fionnuala's arms still around her brothers.

sourceTrail.notes: Mochaomhóg is a fictional character; the Christian ending is generally considered a later addition to an older pre-Christian tale.

characters.name: Aoibh
characters.title: First Wife of Lir
characters.summary: Lir's beloved first wife, mother of the four children — her death sets the tragedy in motion.
characters.plain: Aoibh is Lir's first wife and the mother of Fionnuala, Aodh, Fiachra, and Conn. She dies, and it is her death — and Lir's grief — that leads him to marry her sister Aoife. The tragedy begins with her absence.
characters.description: Aoibh appears only briefly — she dies early — but her shadow lies over everything that follows. Her death is the wound in the family that Lir tries to heal by marrying again too quickly. The choice of her sister Aoife as second wife seemed natural: a woman who already knew and loved the children. But it proves catastrophic. Aoibh's absence is the space into which jealousy grows. She is the loved one whose place cannot be filled, and whose loss indirectly causes nine hundred years of suffering.

sourceTrail.notes: Aoibh's name means 'radiance' or 'beauty.' Some versions spell her name Aobh.

characters.name: Deirdre
characters.title: Most Beautiful Woman in Ireland
characters.summary: The woman whose prophesied beauty brings ruin — who chooses love over safety and pays for it.
characters.plain: Deirdre is prophesied at birth to be the most beautiful woman in Ireland and to bring ruin upon Ulster. Kept hidden by Conchobar until she can be made his queen, she defies him — placing a geis on the warrior Naoise and fleeing to Scotland. When Conchobar lures them back with false promises, she loses everything.
characters.description: Deirdre is one of the great figures of Irish mythology — a woman who sees her fate clearly and walks toward it with open eyes. She knows the prophecy. She knows what will happen if she defies Conchobar. She does it anyway, because she has decided that a life without love is not worth the safety it offers. Her comparison of Naoise to a raven, snow, and blood is one of mythology's most beautiful moments of longing. Her defiance of Conchobar is a form of sovereignty: her life belongs to her. The year of silence she keeps after Naoise's death, refusing to smile, refusing to speak, is the story's most devastating act of resistance.

sourceTrail.primary: Longes mac nUislenn (Exile of the Sons of Uisneach)
sourceTrail.notes: One of the Trí Truaighe na Scéalaíochta — Three Sorrows of Storytelling.

characters.name: Naoise
characters.title: Champion of Ulster, Son of Uisneach
characters.summary: The warrior Deirdre chooses — who knows the prophecy and cannot refuse the geis she lays on him.
characters.plain: Naoise is one of the three sons of Uisneach, renowned fighters of Ulster. When Deirdre lays her geis upon him, he refuses at first — he knows the prophecy — but finds he cannot live with the refusal. He takes her hand and leads her out into the night.
characters.description: Naoise is a hero defined by the bind he cannot escape. He knows, when Deirdre first approaches him, exactly what accepting the geis means: exile, pursuit, and eventual death at the hands of a king who will not forgive. He refuses her. She makes it impossible to refuse. His acceptance is honest — he chooses Deirdre knowing the cost. The years in Scotland are their reward: years of happiness the story presents as real and worth having. When he is killed, it is by treachery, not in fair combat. He dies as a warrior who deserved better.

sourceTrail.notes: Naoise's name is variously spelled Noisiu, Naisi, or Naoise across different manuscripts.

characters.name: Ardán
characters.title: Son of Uisneach
characters.summary: One of Naoise's two brothers who share every year of the exile and die with him.
characters.plain: Ardán is one of the three sons of Uisneach. He and his brother Ainle follow Naoise and Deirdre into exile in Scotland, sharing every year of the flight, and die with their brother when Conchobar's treachery brings them home.
characters.description: Ardán and Ainle are inseparable from Naoise in the story — they are a unit, the three brothers of Uisneach. Their individual personalities are not extensively developed, but their loyalty is absolute. They go into exile knowing what it means. They return to Ireland because Naoise is persuaded to, and Fergus's guarantee seemed to offer a way home. They die together, killed by the same treachery, and are buried together. The story's Irish title names all three equally: Longes mac nUislenn — Exile of the Sons of Uisneach.

characters.name: Ainle
characters.title: Son of Uisneach
characters.summary: Naoise's second brother, who shares the exile and the death at Emain Macha.
characters.plain: Ainle is the third son of Uisneach. Like his brother Ardán, he goes into exile with Naoise and Deirdre, fights at his brothers' side, and dies with them at Emain Macha when Conchobar springs his trap.
characters.description: Ainle completes the threesome of the sons of Uisneach. The Irish title of the story names all three equally — they are exiled together, remembered together. In a society built on loyalty to kin, the brothers' fidelity to each other and to the woman Naoise chose is the value the story celebrates. Their deaths, by treachery rather than in honourable combat, make the loss more bitter.

characters.name: Cathbad
characters.title: Chief Druid of Ulster
characters.summary: Ulster's chief druid — the man who speaks the prophecy that makes Deirdre's fate inevitable.
characters.plain: Cathbad is the chief druid of Ulster, advisor to Conchobar mac Nessa. At the feast where Feidlimid's unborn child cries out from the womb, Cathbad reads the omen and speaks the prophecy: she will be the most beautiful woman in Ireland and the cause of great ruin.
characters.description: Cathbad occupies one of the most ambiguous positions in the Deirdre story. He does not create the prophecy — he reads it, accurately, from an omen he did not summon. His report is not malicious, but its consequence is catastrophic. When Conchobar decides to keep the child rather than kill her, Cathbad does not argue. He appears elsewhere in the Ulster Cycle as a druid of extraordinary power — it is Cathbad who teaches Cú Chulainn's year-cohort, and Cathbad who speaks several of the cycle's most significant prophecies.

sourceTrail.primary: Longes mac nUislenn; also Táin and Macgnímartha Con Culainn
sourceTrail.notes: Cathbad is one of the most frequently appearing figures in the Ulster Cycle.

characters.name: Eoghan mac Durthacht
characters.title: King of Fernmag
characters.summary: The man Conchobar hires to kill Naoise — no Ulster warrior would do it themselves.
characters.plain: Eoghan mac Durthacht is the Ulster king pressed into service as Conchobar's executioner. He kills Naoise and his brothers at Emain Macha when no true Ulster warrior would carry out the act. Conchobar's threat to give Deirdre to Eoghan is the final indignity she escapes by taking her own life.
characters.description: Eoghan mac Durthacht functions in the story as the instrument of Conchobar's revenge — brought in precisely because Ulster's own warriors refused. His role is limited but structurally essential: someone has to kill Naoise, and the story needs that killing to be perceived as dishonourable — executed by a man Naoise had no cause to trust, in a situation he had been promised was safe. Conchobar's subsequent threat to give Deirdre to Eoghan is intended as the final indignity, and Deirdre's response — leaning from the chariot and dashing her head against a rock — makes it the story's final act of sovereignty over her own fate.

characters.name: Feidlimid mac Daill
characters.title: Storyteller to Conchobar
characters.summary: Deirdre's father — the king's storyteller whose unborn daughter cried out and set the prophecy in motion.
characters.plain: Feidlimid mac Daill is Conchobar's storyteller, at whose feast the terrible prophecy is spoken. He is Deirdre's father. When the druid Cathbad reads the omen and declares the ruin she will bring, Feidlimid is helpless — the fate of his daughter is decided at a feast in his own house.
characters.description: Feidlimid is a tragic peripheral figure — a man whose profession is the making and preserving of narratives, who becomes a character in a story he cannot control. The irony of the professional storyteller whose own story ends in disaster is built into his narrative function. He has no power to protect his daughter from the prophecy or from the king who claims her.

characters.name: Gráinne
characters.title: Daughter of the High King of Ireland
characters.summary: The king's daughter who drugs a feast, lays a binding fate on the man she wants, and runs.
characters.plain: Gráinne is the daughter of the High King Cormac mac Airt, promised in marriage to the ageing Fionn mac Cumhaill. At the betrothal feast she sees Diarmuid and decides, with absolute certainty, that she wants him instead. She drugs the hall, lays a geis on him, and flees into sixteen years of pursuit.
characters.description: Gráinne is one of the most vivid personalities in the Fenian cycle — decisive, impulsive, and willing to bear the consequences of her choices. She acts in the feast scene with a speed and clarity that leaves no room for doubt: she knows what she wants, she knows the price, and she pays it. What makes her story complex is what follows: over sixteen years of flight, the geis that bound Diarmuid becomes something else. By the time Fionn arranges Diarmuid's death at Ben Bulben, Gráinne's feelings have become genuine love. Some versions of the story end with Gráinne eventually accepting Fionn's hand — an ending that disturbs readers, and was likely intended to.

sourceTrail.earliest: Oral tradition; main manuscript text 14th century
sourceTrail.notes: Place-names across Ireland mark 'beds of Diarmuid and Gráinne' — resting places from the sixteen-year pursuit.

characters.name: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne
characters.title: Champion of the Fianna
characters.summary: The warrior with the beauty spot that makes every woman love him — who cannot refuse Gráinne's geis.
characters.plain: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne is the finest warrior of the Fianna, foster-son of Aonghus Óg. He bears a love-spot on his forehead that makes any woman who sees it fall helplessly in love. When Gráinne lays her geis on him at the feast, he knows exactly what it means — and goes anyway.
characters.description: Diarmuid is a hero defined by constraint. The love-spot he carries is not a gift — it is a burden. When Gráinne binds him with the geis, he argues, lists every reason he cannot and should not go, makes plain the destruction that will follow — and goes anyway, because the geis leaves him no honourable choice. His sixteen years of running are not cowardly: he leaves signs at every camp to show Fionn he is not sleeping with Gráinne, at least initially. What he cannot prevent is that time and proximity gradually become something he has no category for. His death at Ben Bulben, engineered by the man he had once called leader, is one of the cycle's most bitter conclusions.

sourceTrail.earliest: Oral tradition; main manuscript text 14th century
sourceTrail.notes: The love-spot (ball seirce) motif is consistent across all versions.

characters.name: Fionn mac Cumhaill
characters.title: Leader of the Fianna
characters.summary: The great warrior-poet who gains all wisdom from a fish's skin — and cannot forgive what is done to him at Tara.
characters.plain: Fionn mac Cumhaill is the leader of the Fianna, Ireland's band of elite warriors. As a boy he accidentally tasted the Salmon of Knowledge and gained the ability to perceive any hidden truth. As an old man, his bride-to-be flees him at the feast — and his pursuit of Diarmuid and Gráinne over sixteen years defines the dark side of his greatness.
characters.description: Fionn mac Cumhaill is the central figure of the Fenian Cycle — a hero who appears in dozens of tales spanning his boyhood, prime, and old age. He is simultaneously poet and warrior, lawgiver and hunter, wisdom-keeper and man undone by wounded pride. The Salmon of Knowledge gives him everything: perception, understanding, the ability to see what is hidden. The Tara feast takes from him something no wisdom can recover — his dignity, and the woman he had planned to marry in front of every important person in Ireland. The moment on Ben Bulben when he cups water and lets it run through his fingers twice is one of Irish mythology's most psychologically precise images of a great man making himself small.

sourceTrail.primary: Macgnímartha Find; Tóraíocht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne; Acallam na Senórach
sourceTrail.earliest: Lebor na hUidre contains early Fenian material; major texts 12th–14th century
sourceTrail.oral: Fenian oral tradition — the most active oral tradition in Irish history, surviving into the 20th century
sourceTrail.notes: Fionn mac Cumhaill is the subject of one of the largest bodies of oral narrative in world literature.

characters.name: Cormac mac Airt
characters.title: High King of Ireland
characters.summary: The High King of Ireland, father of Gráinne — powerless when his daughter runs from his feast.
characters.plain: Cormac mac Airt is the legendary High King of Ireland, Gráinne's father, and the host of the feast at Tara where she lays her geis on Diarmuid. He is one of the most celebrated figures in all of Irish legendary history.
characters.description: Cormac mac Airt is one of Ireland's greatest legendary kings — renowned for justice, wisdom, and the splendour of his court — but in the Pursuit he is primarily Gráinne's father, unable to undo what his daughter has done or protect her from its consequences. His willingness to receive Diarmuid and Gráinne back into favour during one of the pursuit's truces suggests he is not entirely in Fionn's camp. He is the man in the middle, watching a conflict he cannot resolve.

sourceTrail.primary: Tóraíocht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne; also many independent tales
sourceTrail.earliest: Cormac appears in texts from the 8th century onward
sourceTrail.notes: Cormac mac Airt is a semi-legendary figure associated with the 3rd century CE. His historicity is debated.

characters.name: Aonghus Óg
characters.title: God of Love and Youth
characters.summary: The god of love who fostered Diarmuid and shelters the fugitives with his divine protection.
characters.plain: Aonghus Óg is the son of the Dagda and Bóinn, god of love, youth, and poetry, who dwells at Brú na Bóinne — Newgrange. He fostered Diarmuid from childhood and is his divine protector. When Diarmuid and Gráinne are hunted, Aonghus intervenes on their behalf.
characters.description: Aonghus Óg is one of the Tuatha Dé's most beloved figures — the god who wanders at night with four birds over his head (his kisses transformed into birds), who loves with absolute selflessness. His role in the Pursuit is as Diarmuid's foster-father and protector. He shelters Gráinne under his own cloak when Fionn's forces close in. He cannot prevent Diarmuid's eventual death — some fates are outside even a god's power — but he carries the body to Brú na Bóinne, where he breathes a kind of intermittent life into it and can still speak with it.

sourceTrail.primary: Tóraíocht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne; also Aisling Óenguso (Dream of Aonghus)
sourceTrail.earliest: Aisling Óenguso preserved in 9th–10th century texts
sourceTrail.notes: Aonghus Óg's dwelling at Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange) is consistent across many texts.

characters.name: The Boar of Ben Bulben
characters.title: Diarmuid's Doom
characters.summary: The enchanted boar that is Diarmuid's fate-bond — whose poisoned bristles kill him on Ben Bulben.
characters.plain: The Boar of Ben Bulben is an enchanted beast — in truth, Diarmuid's own foster-brother, transformed by supernatural forces. There is a fate-bond between them: neither can survive the other. Fionn knows this when he arranges the hunt. Diarmuid kills the boar — and the boar's poisoned bristles rake his foot as it dies.
characters.description: The Boar of Ben Bulben is the instrument of Diarmuid's fate, but also a victim. The story behind the boar — that it is the reincarnation of Diarmuid's foster-brother, transformed by the same supernatural forces that gave Diarmuid his love-spot — makes it a figure of tragedy rather than merely menace. The fate-bond between them is one of Irish mythology's recurrent patterns: two beings linked across lifetimes, their collision inevitable. Fionn's knowledge of this bond, and his decision to arrange the hunt anyway, is what transforms his character in this final act.

sourceTrail.earliest: Oral tradition; main manuscript text 14th century
sourceTrail.notes: The boar's backstory varies across versions. In some tellings it is Roc, Aonghus Óg's steward, whose son was transformed by his father's dying curse.

characters.name: Oisín
characters.title: Poet-Warrior of the Fianna
characters.summary: Fionn's son, poet of the Fianna, who rides west into the immortal world and returns to find three centuries gone.
characters.plain: Oisín is the son of Fionn mac Cumhaill and the greatest poet of the Fianna. When the goddess Niamh rides out of the western sea and asks him to come with her to Tír na nÓg, he goes. He lives there for what feels like three years. When he returns to Ireland, three centuries have passed and everything he knew is gone.
characters.description: Oisín is one of Irish mythology's most poignant figures — the witness across time, the man who outlives his own world. His three centuries in Tír na nÓg are not presented as a mistake or a fall — he is genuinely happy there, genuinely loves Niamh. What draws him back is a homesickness for Ireland that the immortal world, for all its perfection, cannot cure. When he falls from the horse and the centuries catch up with him, his final task is transmission of memory: in the Acallam na Senórach, he walks through Ireland with St Patrick, telling stories of every place they pass. Everything he describes is already archaeology. He is the last living container of a world that has ceased to exist.

sourceTrail.primary: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg (by Micheál Coimín, c. 1750); Acallam na Senórach (c. 1200 CE)
sourceTrail.oral: Fenian oral tradition, active in Ireland and Scotland into the 20th century
sourceTrail.notes: The Laoi Oisín, the most familiar form, was written in the 18th century but synthesises a very old oral tradition.

characters.name: Niamh of the Golden Hair
characters.title: Princess of Tír na nÓg
characters.summary: The radiant woman from the land beyond the western sea who rides to Ireland for Fionn's son.
characters.plain: Niamh of the Golden Hair is a daughter of the king of Tír na nÓg — the Land of Eternal Youth beyond the western sea. She rides to Ireland on a white horse to seek Oisín, whom she has watched from afar. She promises him a world without age or sorrow, and she keeps her word.
characters.description: Niamh is one of Irish mythology's great love figures — generous, real, and given very little narrative space to be any of these things. She comes to Ireland specifically for Oisín, specifically because she has chosen him. She gives him everything she promises. When he wants to leave, she releases him, despite knowing what it means: that he will not come back as himself. Her final warning — do not touch Irish soil — is an act of love that he cannot honour, not because it is difficult but because the moment arrives too fast.

sourceTrail.primary: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg; Acallam na Senórach
sourceTrail.notes: Niamh's characterisation is more developed in the 18th-century Laoi Oisín than in earlier sources.

characters.name: St. Patrick
characters.title: Apostle of Ireland
characters.summary: The saint who finds the ancient poet Oisín and listens to the last stories of the Fianna.
characters.plain: St Patrick appears in the Fenian Cycle as the recorder of Oisín's stories. When Oisín falls and becomes an ancient man, it is Patrick who finds him and listens — writing down the tales of a world that no longer exists.
characters.description: Patrick's role in the Oisín narrative is structural and symbolic. He is the new Ireland — the Christian era that has grown over the old heroic world in the three centuries Oisín was away. In the Acallam na Senórach, both Patrick and surviving Fianna warriors walk through Ireland together, with Patrick recording stories of every place they pass. Patrick in the Acallam is not dismissive of the old world — he values the stories and sees their preservation as important. He is a bridge between two Irelands, not a destroyer of the first one.

sourceTrail.primary: Acallam na Senórach (Colloquy of the Ancients, c. 1200 CE)
sourceTrail.oral: Fenian oral tradition with Christian literary framing
sourceTrail.notes: The historical Patrick (c. 385–461 CE) could not have met anyone from the Fenian period; the combination is a mythological literary device.

characters.name: Niamh's White Horse
nameAlternate: The Enchanted Horse of Tír na nÓg
characters.title: The Horse from the Western Sea
characters.summary: The immortal white horse that carries Oisín to Tír na nÓg — and cannot bring him back.
characters.plain: Niamh's white horse comes out of the western sea and returns to it carrying both riders. It preserves Oisín's immortality as long as he stays in the saddle on Irish ground. When the saddle-girth breaks and Oisín falls to earth, the horse turns and gallops west into the sea without him, and is gone.
characters.description: The white horse is a recurring figure in Irish and Celtic mythology as a vehicle between worlds — the natural element of the sovereignty goddess, the creature that crosses the boundary between mortal Ireland and the immortal west. In Oisín's story it functions as a mobile boundary: while Oisín sits on the horse, he remains outside of time's reach. The horse's departure after his fall is the moment the boundary closes permanently. It cannot take back someone who has already touched the mortal ground.

sourceTrail.primary: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg
sourceTrail.notes: The white horse motif appears in sovereignty goddess mythology across the Celtic tradition.

characters.name: Finnegas
characters.title: Druid-Poet of the Boyne
characters.summary: The poet who waited seven years for the Salmon of Knowledge — only to have a boy's burned thumb take everything.
characters.plain: Finnegas is a druid-poet who has spent seven years fishing a pool of the River Boyne, waiting for the Salmon of Knowledge. He hires a clever boy to help him. When the salmon is finally caught, a blister on its skin and an instinctive gesture change whose destiny it was.
characters.description: Finnegas is a figure of tremendous patience and genuine wisdom, undone by the smallest accident. He has given seven years to a single purpose and is within moments of receiving everything he sacrificed those years for. His response when he understands what has happened — when he looks at the boy's face and sees knowledge already there — is one of the story's most moving moments. He does not rage or grieve; he asks the boy's real name, receives it, and gives him the rest of the fish. He accepts the loss with a grace that is itself a form of wisdom, and vanishes from the story having transmitted, inadvertently, everything he had.

sourceTrail.earliest: Preserved in Book of Leinster tradition (c. 1150 CE)

characters.name: The Salmon of Knowledge
characters.title: Repository of All Wisdom
characters.summary: The fish that ate the hazelnuts of all wisdom — and carries everything knowable inside its flesh.
characters.plain: The Salmon of Knowledge lives in the pool of the Well of Segais at the source of the River Boyne. It ate the nine hazelnuts of wisdom that fell from the sacred trees above the well and absorbed every piece of knowledge they contained. Whoever eats the first taste of this fish receives all that wisdom.
characters.description: The Salmon of Knowledge is one of the oldest and most persistent figures in Irish mythological tradition — a creature that precedes the human cycle entirely. Its existence encodes a theory of knowledge: wisdom is not accumulated through study or experience but concentrated in a single object, swallowed whole from the source of all rivers. The nine hazel trees above the Well of Segais represent a complete cosmology. The salmon's role is to be the vessel of inherited universal knowledge waiting for the right inheritor — not necessarily the one who waited longest, nor the one who caught the fish, but the one whose nature was already aligned with what the knowledge contained.

sourceTrail.earliest: Preserved in Book of Leinster tradition (c. 1150 CE)
sourceTrail.oral: Pre-Christian cosmological tradition — older than the Fenian Cycle proper
sourceTrail.notes: The Well of Segais and Salmon of Knowledge motif also appear in Welsh mythology (the salmon of Llyn Llyw in Culhwch and Olwen) and may represent a common Celtic inheritance.
